source.title: Changes in sprint performance and sagittal plane kinematics after heavy resisted sprint training in professional soccer players

paper.citation: Lahti J., Huuhka T., Romero V., Bezodis I., Morin J.B., Häkkinen K. Changes in sprint performance and sagittal plane kinematics after heavy resisted sprint training in professional soccer players. PeerJ. 2020;8:e10507. doi:10.7717/peerj.10507.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Do nine weeks of heavy sled sprinting at 50% or 60% velocity decrement improve sprint performance and mechanics compared with normal training in professional soccer players? Participants: 32 male Finnish Premier League players, age 24.1±5.1 years, height 180±10 cm, mass 76.7±7.7 kg. Sport and level: Professional male soccer; goalkeepers excluded. Design: Nonrandomized pre/post, three-group team-based experiment. Exposure or intervention: Fifteen training opportunities over nine weeks, with individually loaded sleds producing 50% or 60% maximal-velocity decrement, followed by a two-week taper.
paper.tldr: HS50% improved 10 m by 3.37% (2.14±0.06 to 2.07±0.06 s, p<.001, d=-1.25), 20 m by 3.07% (p<.001, d=-1.15), and 30 m by 2.89% (p<.001, d=-1.18). HS60% improved 10 m by 3.05% (p=.001, d=-.96), 20 m by 2.45% (p=.008, d=-.77), and 30 m by 2.04% (p=.021, d=-.62). Individually loaded heavy sled sprinting can be a pragmatic acceleration stimulus, with the 50% decrement showing the clearest 10-m advantage here.
paper.methods: Design: Nonrandomized pre/post, three-group team-based experiment. Exposure or intervention: Fifteen training opportunities over nine weeks, with individually loaded sleds producing 50% or 60% maximal-velocity decrement, followed by a two-week taper. Comparator: Control team continued normal training without systematic acceleration or resisted-sprint work. Measurements and outcomes: 5-, 10-, 20-, and 30-m splits; radar-derived sprint force–velocity profile; manually digitized 2D sagittal kinematics and spatiotemporal variables. Analysis: Baseline-adjusted within/between-group tests, effect sizes, and comparison with between-session minimal detectable change.
paper.findings: HS50% improved 10 m by 3.37% (2.14±0.06 to 2.07±0.06 s, p<.001, d=-1.25), 20 m by 3.07% (p<.001, d=-1.15), and 30 m by 2.89% (p<.001, d=-1.18). HS60% improved 10 m by 3.05% (p=.001, d=-.96), 20 m by 2.45% (p=.008, d=-.77), and 30 m by 2.04% (p=.021, d=-.62). Only the 10-m change showed a group×time interaction (F(2,24)=4.031, p=.031); HS50% improved more than control (p=.03, d=1.03). Both sled groups improved F0, 10-m mean force ratio, and Pmax, but F0 changes (7.83% and 9.23%) remained below the 9.53% between-session MDC. Observed technique fluctuations remained below the minimal detectable change and did not support longitudinal technical breakdown.
paper.limitations: Intervention and control were different teams with different training/recovery cultures; no randomized unloaded-acceleration control. Small groups may have been underpowered; 2D kinematics used only two instants and lower-resolution video, with wide ICC confidence intervals. Professional soccer transfer to NCAA American football is limited by sport demands, calendar, and exposure. Additional causal limitation — interpretation: Team allocation and concurrent training prevent clean attribution of all changes to sled loading.
paper.practicalImplications: Individually loaded heavy sled sprinting can be a pragmatic acceleration stimulus, with the 50% decrement showing the clearest 10-m advantage here. Treat the 50% versus 60% contrast as provisional, monitor actual split-time change against test error, and do not infer that unchanged 2D snapshots prove technique is unaffected in every athlete or task.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, individually loaded heavy sled sprinting can be a pragmatic acceleration stimulus, with the 50% decrement showing the clearest 10-m advantage here. Treat the 50% versus 60% contrast as provisional, monitor actual split-time change against test error, and do not infer that unchanged 2D snapshots prove technique is unaffected in every athlete or task. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, individually loaded heavy sled sprinting can be a pragmatic acceleration stimulus, with the 50% decrement showing the clearest 10-m advantage here. Treat the 50% versus 60% contrast as provisional, monitor actual split-time change against test error, and do not infer that unchanged 2D snapshots prove technique is unaffected in every athlete or task. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
